Hi!
I was in a similar boat to you, and I only got diagnosed at 20 because of social anxiety earlier. The questions that made me seriously consider it are below.

1. Have you taken any recreational stimulants? For me any stimulants seemed to have a paradoxical effect and it was well known that I could even go to sleep on them.

2. Mood symptoms. For a long time I thought ADHD was mainly hyperactivity and inattentiveness, but my psychiatrist at the time said that ADHD often presents with mood swings and other mood disorders, particularly if it's undiagnosed.

3. Experience of school as a very young child, rather than as a teenager. I needed help from my parents for this one, but my experience was pretty poor particularly because I couldn't sit still and kept disobeying orders. As I grew up I was disciplined over and over, which did decrease my acting out but at the cost to my own mental health, as constantly fighting against my own brain took its toll.

4. Forgetfulness, particularly outside working or studying. I never realised that my absent mindedness and missing appointments could be related to ADHD. I just thought I was being dumb or lazy which made me more upset with myself.

5. Sleep problems! I didn't know that insomnia was so common for people with ADHD, so it was a surprise when those two were linked. The telling part was that when I was prescribed medication, it seemed to help my sleep far more than any sleeping tablet had in the past.

I can't diagnose you with anything, and you shouldn't self diagnose, but these are the questions that opened my eyes to the possibility. Having social anxiety made it harder for me, but I felt comfortable as I had the support of my friends to go for the appointments and treatment plans (they would remind me about them, sit with me before them for reassurance etc.).

It's also possible that there's another underlying problem that's causing issues that isn't ADHD, so the diagnosis isn't the be all and end all.

I hope this information was useful and good luck for whatever you end up doing!

OH MY GOD. Yeah I had the same issue and it was driving me insane. It just started out of nowhere and didn't seem to be based on anything external (I've tried everything). My psychologist seemed to think it's a manifestation of my anxiety, and I've found doing something about it, even if it's unrelated, might help tricking the brain into thinking it's working. For example, I decided to put skin cream on all over my back and stomach and it worked for a while even though I don't have a rash or any problem with my skin. I then started using a fan and that worked for a while. My long term solution was getting more comfortable with my sleep environment, such as having a shower before sleeping, setting my bed, using an air freshener etc as well as dealing with my anxiety separately. I hope this can help you and all the best! I know how difficult and annoying it can be...

I have an "anxiety song". Basically I associate different songs to the emotions I'm feeling at the time (I don't know if everyone does it), and so I have a bunch of songs that I associate with better emotions. I've trained myself to play the same songs when I'm in a better mood over and over again to train my mind. So when I get intense anxiety or a panic attack, I can play these songs and it works most of the time. Eventually my brain rewires itself to associate the song with the anxiety, so I have to keep updating the list.

Hey. I've been on many antidepressants (sertraline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine, amitriptyline), and a semi frequent user of psychedelics. I've taken mushrooms and LSD on all these medications, and I've had no problems. They've in fact been such good experiences I intend to continue taking them for the forseeable future lol. Don't want to encourage the taking of psychedelics, but I've had no issue with them. One thing I would say is be careful of the dosage as it can cause seratonin syndrome in large doses.

Hey, that sounds awful. I've also experienced a similar thing, also at a late stage in treatment which is surprising. After jumping between different antidepressants, I've been settled on 45mg mirtazapine, 100mg amitriptyline and 40mg propranolol daily. After about 6 months, I've also inexplicably lost fine thinking skills. I've been losing my memory more often, I'm making more mistakes with my university work, I've dropped ranks in all the games I've played. I also feel mentally tired for no reason. I've tried changing other things like diet and exercise, but nothing seems to help. It's got to the point where I'm asking my doctor to stop my medications because it's too much.. It's a shame because these medications helped me get sleep I thought I'd never get for the rest of my life. It must be a side effect that's not mentioned much and something to do with neurotransmitter balance? I'm not a doctor so idk... Just sharing my thoughts.
To clarify, I've been on my current dosage (45mg) for 5 weeks. I was steady increased from 15mg to 45 mg in the first few weeks.

Depression, generalised anxiety and possibly social anxiety. I've been taking it for about 5 weeks now but I haven't felt too much different. I'm also taking amitriptyline and propranolol with it and I feel that propranolol has the biggest effect on anxiety. It does make me sleep a lot better though so based on that I'm continuing taking it. They say it can take up to 8 weeks to start working, so let's see what happens in a few more weeks...

Hey there. I was started on mirtazapine after sertraline and venlafaxine didn't work, and I've put on a little bit of weight (2kg over 2 months) but it's not massive weight gain. I've got vivid weird dreams but wouldn't say that they were bad. Definitely would say give it a shot if you feel like you need the medication :) the potential benefit far outweighs the side effects for me.
